subChunks.title: Geochemistry & Earth Systems Science
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora picked up a small piece of granite and turned it over. “This rock is approximately 300 million years old. It contains uranium-238, which decays to lead-206 with a half-life of 4.47 billion years. From the ratio of uranium to lead in this sample, we can calculate precisely when this granite crystallised from magma. Geochemistry gives us a chronometer written in radioactive decay — so accurate we can date lunar samples to within a few million years out of 4.5 billion.”

Geochemistry is the study of the chemical composition and processes of Earth — how elements cycle through the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere; how isotope ratios record past environments; how chemical reactions control rock formation, weathering, and the composition of seawater. Earth systems science extends this to understand Earth as an integrated system: biogeochemical cycles linking life to geology, the long-term carbon cycle that stabilised Earthís climate over billions of years, and the feedbacks that govern habitability.

At SENIOR level, geochemistry requires both quantitative skill (isotope calculations, mass balance, decay equations) and systems thinking — understanding how chemical cycles interact and how human activity is disrupting equilibria that evolved over geological time.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Radiometric Dating

Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics: N(t) = N₀e^(−λt), where N₀ is the initial number of parent atoms, N is the remaining parent atoms at time t, and λ is the decay constant (λ = ln 2 / t₁/₂). Since daughter atoms D = N₀ − N, the age equation is: t = (1/λ) × ln(1 + D/N). Different isotope systems span different time ranges and are suitable for different materials:

  • U-Pb (uranium-lead): ²³⁸U → ²⁰⁶Pb (t₁/₂ = 4.47 Ga) and ²³⁵U → ²⁰⁷Pb (t₁/₂ = 0.704 Ga). Concordia diagrams plot ²⁰⁷Pb/²³⁵U vs ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U — samples that have remained closed systems fall on the concordia curve; discordance indicates Pb loss or gain. Used for zircon crystals in igneous and metamorphic rocks; provides the oldest reliable ages (Jack Hills zircons, 4.4 Ga).
  • K-Ar and Ar-Ar: ⁴⁰K → ⁴⁰Ar (t₁/₂ = 1.25 Ga). Suitable for K-rich minerals (muscovite, sanidine, hornblende) and volcanic rocks. Ar-Ar (using neutron irradiation to convert ³⁹K to ³⁹Ar) allows incremental heating to identify disturbed samples.
  • Rb-Sr: ⁸⁷Rb → ⁸⁷Sr (t₁/₂ = 48.8 Ga). Isochron method corrects for initial Sr — a suite of co-genetic rocks with different Rb/Sr ratios, when plotted on a ⁸⁷Rb/⁸⁶Sr vs ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr isochron diagram, yields a line whose slope gives the age.
  • ¹⁴C radiocarbon: t₁/₂ = 5,730 years. Useful for organic material <50,000 years old. ¹⁴C is produced in the atmosphere by cosmic ray spallation of ¹⁴N; living organisms maintain equilibrium with atmospheric ¹⁴C; after death, decay begins. Calibration against tree rings (dendrochronology) and coral corrects for past variations in atmospheric ¹⁴C production.

Stable Isotope Geochemistry

Stable isotopes (no radioactive decay) fractionate according to thermodynamic and kinetic processes — heavier isotopes concentrate in phases with stronger bonds. Fractionation is expressed as δ notation: δ¹⁸O (‰) = [(¹⁸O/¹⁶O)_sample / (¹⁸O/¹⁶O)_standard − 1] × 1000.

δ¹⁸O in carbonates: At higher temperatures, ¹⁸O fractionation into carbonate (relative to seawater) decreases — so warmer waters produce lower δ¹⁸O in marine carbonates and vice versa. Foraminifera shells preserved in ocean sediment cores are a paleothermometer — the oscillations in δ¹⁸O through glacial-interglacial cycles (Marine Isotope Stages) reflect both temperature changes and the growth and melting of ice sheets (ice is ¹⁸O-depleted, so glacial periods have higher seawater δ¹⁸O).

δ¹³C: Photosynthesis preferentially incorporates ¹²CO₂ (lighter), so organic matter has lower δ¹³C than inorganic carbon. Negative δ¹³C excursions in carbonate records indicate large inputs of ¹²C-rich carbon (from organic carbon oxidation, methane hydrate release, or volcanism) and are associated with major carbon cycle perturbations (e.g. Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous ocean anoxic events).

The Long-Term Carbon Cycle and Climate Stability

The deep-time stability of Earth’s climate (liquid water present for >3.8 Ga despite the Sun being ~30% less luminous in the early Hadean) is maintained by the long-term carbon cycle — a geochemical thermostat operating on million-year timescales:

Silicate weathering: CO₂ + CaSiO₃ + H₂O → CaCO₃ + SiO₂ + H₂O. Atmospheric CO₂ reacts with silicate minerals in rain (carbonic acid formation), transporting HCO₃⁻ to the ocean, where carbonate is precipitated and buried as limestone. Warmer temperatures accelerate weathering (faster chemical kinetics), drawing down more CO₂ — a negative feedback that has kept Earth’s climate within habitable bounds over billions of years (the Urey-Walker-Berner GEOCARB model).

Volcanic/metamorphic outgassing: Subducted carbonate is returned as CO₂ by metamorphism and volcanic outgassing. The balance between silicate weathering (drawdown) and volcanism (input) determines long-term atmospheric CO₂ levels. Higher sea-floor spreading rates increase volcanic CO₂ inputs and warm the climate; Himalayan uplift accelerated weathering and may have cooled Cenozoic climate.

The Faint Young Sun paradox: If CO₂ and other greenhouse gases were higher in the early atmosphere, the reduced solar luminosity could have been compensated — but direct evidence remains contested. Methane may have played a larger role in early Archean warming.

Biogeochemical Cycles — Human Perturbation

The nitrogen cycle: Biological nitrogen fixation (by diazotrophs like Rhizobium, Azotobacter, and cyanobacteria) is the primary natural input of reactive nitrogen to ecosystems (~120 Tg N/yr). The Haber-Bosch process for industrial ammonia synthesis now fixes ~120 Tg N/yr additionally — doubling the global flux of reactive nitrogen. Consequences: eutrophication of coastal waters (Gulf of Mexico dead zone), nitrous oxide emissions (N₂O, a potent greenhouse gas and ozone destroyer), and ecosystem nitrogen saturation altering plant community composition.

The phosphorus cycle: Unlike nitrogen and carbon, phosphorus has no significant gaseous phase — it moves through the lithosphere and hydrosphere only. Weathering of phosphate rocks and biological decomposition are the main fluxes. Mining of phosphate rock (for fertiliser) is depleting geological reserves — some estimates project economically recoverable reserves lasting <300 years. Phosphate is non-substitutable for agriculture; its sustainable management is an underappreciated global challenge.

Ocean acidification chemistry: Dissolution of anthropogenic CO₂ in seawater: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → 2H⁺ + CO₃²⁻. Since pre-industrial times, ocean pH has dropped from ~8.2 to ~8.1 — a 26% increase in [H⁺] (pH is logarithmic). Aragonite and calcite saturation states (Ω) are declining — below Ω = 1, shells and skeletons dissolve. The Southern Ocean is projected to become undersaturated with respect to aragonite by 2030–2050 under high-emissions scenarios, threatening pteropods, oysters, and coral reefs far earlier than warming alone.

storyBeats.text: Theodora drew the Urey reaction on the board — CO₂ plus CaSiO₃ yielding calcium carbonate and silica. “This reaction, running over millions of years, is why Earth hasn’t become Venus. Venus has the same amount of carbon as Earth — but it all stayed as CO₂ in the atmosphere. On Earth, it got weathered into rock. The difference is liquid water. One molecule.”
“So the silicate weathering thermostat — if temperatures rise, weathering accelerates, CO₂ is drawn down, temperatures fall. It’s a negative feedback on geological timescales?”

“Exactly. But the timescale is the key: it operates over hundreds of thousands to millions of years. It cannot compensate for human CO₂ emissions on human timescales — those act in decades, and the weathering feedback is millions of years too slow. We’ve moved the carbon cycle faster than any geological event except perhaps the most violent large igneous province eruptions. The planet will recover — in a few hundred thousand years. That is cold comfort.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how radiocarbon dating works — from why living things have ¹⁴C in them, to why the ¹⁴C decreases after death, to how you calculate an age from what’s left. Include why it can’t be used for very old rocks.
learningObjectives: Apply the radioactive decay equation to calculate age from parent-daughter ratios, selecting appropriate isotopic systems for different materials and age ranges
Interpret δ¹⁸O and δ¹³C records from marine sediment cores in terms of paleoclimate and carbon cycle perturbations
Explain the silicate weathering-volcanic outgassing thermostat mechanism that stabilises Earth’s long-term climate, and evaluate its relevance to current anthropogenic CO₂ emissions
Quantify the human perturbation to the nitrogen cycle (Haber-Bosch) and the ocean carbonate chemistry impact of acidification, connecting these to specific ecological consequences
commonMistakes: Confusing the long-term carbon cycle (silicate weathering thermostat, operating on Ma timescales) with the short-term carbon cycle (photosynthesis/respiration/ocean exchange, operating on years to centuries)

Applying radiocarbon dating to materials older than ~50,000 years — only ~8 half-lives remain, making the residual ¹⁴C below detection limits; U-Pb or other long-lived systems must be used for older materials

Interpreting a 0.1 unit drop in ocean pH as ‘small’ — pH is logarithmic, and a drop of 0.1 represents a 26% increase in [H⁺] concentration, with substantial chemical consequences for carbonate saturation

Treating isochron dates as straightforward ages without considering closed-system requirements — the date is only valid if the system has remained closed to parent and daughter element movement since crystallisation
assessmentCriteria: Can use the decay equation N = N₀e^(−λt) or the age equation t = (1/λ)ln(1 + D/N) to solve for age given isotopic ratios, and can explain what the isochron method adds over simple parent-daughter ratios
Can interpret a δ¹⁸O record from a foraminifera core — identifying glacial/interglacial cycles, explaining the dual temperature and ice volume signal, and linking excursions to known events
Can trace the biogeochemical pathway from industrial nitrogen fixation to coastal hypoxia — identifying each transformation step and the organisms or processes involved
Can calculate the change in ocean [H⁺] from a given pH change and explain why carbonate saturation state matters for calcifying marine organisms
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A zircon crystal is found in a metamorphic rock. Mass spectrometry gives: ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U ratio = 0.0835. The half-life of ²³⁸U is 4.468 × 10⁹ years. Use the age equation t = (1/λ) × ln(1 + ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U) where D/N = ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U (assuming no initial ²⁰⁶Pb in the zircon crystal at the time of crystallisation).

  1. Calculate the decay constant λ for ²³⁸U.
  2. Calculate the age of the zircon in years.
  3. A second zircon from the same outcrop gives a ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U ratio of 0.0842 but shows zoning under cathodoluminescence, suggesting it has complex growth history. How should this information change your interpretation of the second date?
  4. The rock also contains muscovite, which is dated by Ar-Ar at 250 Ma. Suggest a geological scenario that could explain U-Pb zircon dates of ~550 Ma but Ar-Ar muscovite dates of ~250 Ma in the same rock.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Decay constant λ:
λ = ln 2 / t₁/₂ = 0.6931 / (4.468 × 10⁹ yr) = 1.551 × 10⁻¹⁰ yr⁻¹

2. Age of zircon:
t = (1/λ) × ln(1 + D/N) = (1 / 1.551 × 10⁻¹⁰) × ln(1 + 0.0835)
= (6.447 × 10⁹) × ln(1.0835)
= (6.447 × 10⁹) × 0.08020
= 5.17 × 10⁸ years ≈ 517 Ma (early Cambrian)

3. Zoned second zircon:
Cathodoluminescence (CL) zoning in zircon indicates multiple growth episodes — the zircon grew in more than one phase, possibly with a metamorphic overgrowth surrounding an older core. The measured bulk ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U ratio would then be a mixed age — a weighted average of the original crystallisation age and the overgrowth age. This ratio should not be interpreted as a single event age. The correct approach is to analyse core and rim separately by SHRIMP or LA-ICPMS (in situ isotope analysis), which can resolve the two ages spatially. The apparent discordance between the two zircon ages (517 Ma vs a slightly different age from the second) may also reflect Pb loss or gain — a concordia diagram would reveal this if both ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U and ²⁰⁷Pb/²³⁵U ratios are measured.

4. U-Pb 517 Ma vs Ar-Ar 250 Ma scenario:
The zircon U-Pb age records the time of crystallisation from magma or metamorphic recrystallisation at 517 Ma. The muscovite Ar-Ar age records the time when the muscovite cooled below its argon closure temperature (~300–350°C for muscovite). A geological scenario consistent with both ages: (i) the original rock formed or underwent high-grade metamorphism at ~517 Ma (zircon formed or was completely re-set at this time); (ii) the rock subsequently remained buried and hot for ~270 million years (perhaps in the lower crust of an orogenic belt), during which ⁴⁰Ar produced from K decay diffused out of muscovite (open system); (iii) at ~250 Ma, the rock cooled through the muscovite Ar closure temperature — perhaps during exhumation and erosion of an overlying mountain belt — at which point muscovite began retaining ⁴⁰Ar. The Ar-Ar date therefore records the cooling/exhumation age, not the original crystallisation age. This scenario of multi-stage thermal history is common in deeply buried metamorphic rocks.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The ‘great oxidation event’ (GOE), approximately 2.4 billion years ago, was one of the most transformative geochemical events in Earth’s history — when atmospheric oxygen rose from near-zero to detectable levels, fundamentally changing surface chemistry and opening new evolutionary possibilities. Evaluate: (a) what geochemical evidence records the GOE; (b) what drove the GOE biologically and geologically; (c) what the geochemical consequences were for ocean and land chemistry; and (d) what the GOE implies about the detectability of life on exoplanets via atmospheric biosignatures.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Geochemical evidence for the GOE:
Multiple independent proxies record the GOE: (i) Mass-independent fractionation of sulfur isotopes (MIF-S): before 2.4 Ga, sulfur isotopes in ancient sediments show MIF-S signal, which can only exist if atmospheric SO₂ was UV-photolysed without an ozone screen. After 2.4 Ga, MIF-S disappears — indicating an ozone layer had developed, requiring O₂ levels above ~10⁻⁵ PAL (present atmospheric level). This is the most precise geochemical marker. (ii) Detrital uraninite and pyrite: before the GOE, these easily oxidised minerals appear as sedimentary grains — impossible after oxygenation because they react with oxygen. Their disappearance from sediments after ~2.4 Ga records oxidation. (iii) Red beds: oxidised iron-rich continental sediments appear globally after 2.4 Ga — the iron has been oxidised to Fe³⁺. (iv) Banded iron formations (BIFs): these massive iron oxide deposits, common before 2.4 Ga, require alternating reduced and oxidised iron delivery to the ocean — consistent with episodic oxygenation. Their decline after the GOE reflects more sustained oxygenation oxidising dissolved Fe²⁺ in the ocean.

(b) Drivers of the GOE:
The biological driver was oxygenic photosynthesis — the evolution of cyanobacteria capable of splitting water to produce O₂ as a byproduct. Molecular phylogenetic analyses suggest cyanobacteria evolved well before the GOE (~3.0–2.7 Ga), so why did O₂ not rise earlier? The geological explanation involves O₂ ‘oxygen sinks’: (i) early Earth had abundant reduced volcanic gases (H₂, H₂S, SO₂) that consumed O₂ as fast as cyanobacteria produced it; (ii) methane produced by archaea may have maintained a reducing greenhouse; (iii) reduced iron in the ocean consumed photosynthetically produced O₂. The GOE may have been triggered by a decline in volcanic degassing rates (reducing the reductant flux from volcanism), gradual accumulation of photosynthetic biomass (burying reduced carbon, leaving oxidised O₂), and changes in continental weathering. The exact trigger remains debated.

(c) Geochemical consequences:
(i) Ocean chemistry transformed: dissolved Fe²⁺ was oxidised to insoluble Fe³⁺ and precipitated (explaining the end of major BIF deposition); manganese was oxidised; hydrogen sulfide in the deep ocean was oxidised over subsequent hundreds of millions of years (though the deep ocean remained anoxic until the Ediacaran, ~580 Ma). (ii) Land surface chemistry: minerals previously stable in the reducing atmosphere (pyrite, uraninite) began weathering rapidly, releasing sulfate and uranium into rivers; continental weathering rates changed. (iii) The ‘Snowball Earth’ episodes (~2.4 and 2.2 Ga) may have been partly triggered by GOE — destruction of methane (a potent greenhouse gas) by O₂ could have collapsed the methane greenhouse, causing runaway glaciation. (iv) The stratospheric ozone layer formed, shielding land surfaces from UV radiation and eventually enabling colonisation of land.

(d) Implications for exoplanet biosignatures:
The GOE illustrates several important points for astrobiology: (i) O₂ is a biosignature — no known abiotic process produces atmospheric O₂ at detectable levels for geological timescales; (ii) but life existed on Earth for ~1.5–2 billion years before O₂ was detectable in the atmosphere — a planet could support abundant life without a detectable O₂ signal (as early Earth demonstrates); (iii) the combination of O₂ + CH₄ is a particularly strong biosignature because these gases are thermodynamically incompatible — in an abiotic system they would react; coexistence implies active production of both by biology; (iv) the false negative problem: we might examine a habitable planet hosting abundant anoxygenic photosynthetic life and conclude it is lifeless, as pre-GOE Earth would have appeared. Detection of biosignatures on exoplanets via atmospheric spectroscopy (as planned for JWST and future large space telescopes) must account for this evolutionary dimension — the absence of O₂ does not mean the absence of life.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A two-dimensional plot of ²⁰⁷Pb/²³⁵U vs ²⁰⁶Pb/²³⁸U values, on which samples that have remained closed systems throughout their history should fall — called the concordia curve. Samples that have lost Pb (or gained U) after formation plot off the concordia; a line through discordant analyses intersects the concordia at the original crystallisation age (upper intercept) and the age of Pb loss (lower intercept).

Massive outpourings of magma covering >100,000 km² — including flood basalts (Deccan Traps, Siberian Traps, Columbia River Basalts) and oceanic plateaux. LIPs have been associated with mass extinction events through volcanogenic CO₂, SO₂ aerosols, and ocean anoxia. The Siberian Traps coincide with the Permian-Triassic mass extinction; the Deccan Traps erupted around the K-Pg boundary.

A measure of the degree of chemical weathering in sedimentary rocks — based on the relative depletion of mobile cations (Na, K, Ca) compared to immobile Al during weathering. Higher CIA values indicate more intense chemical weathering, which is temperature- and moisture-dependent — used as a paleoclimate proxy in ancient sedimentary sequences.

Periods in the Neoproterozoic (~710 and ~635 Ma) when evidence suggests global glaciation reached tropical latitudes — preserved in glacial diamictites with low palaeomagnetic latitudes and extreme δ¹³C excursions. The escape from Snowball Earth is proposed to involve volcanic CO₂ buildup to ~0.1 atm (without silicate weathering operating on ice-covered continents), triggering rapid deglaciation and extreme weathering.

Periods of widespread ocean deoxygenation recorded as black shale horizons with distinctive negative δ¹³C excursions — reflecting large inputs of ¹²C-rich carbon (usually attributed to LIP volcanism) and burial of organic-rich sediments. Major OAEs in the Cretaceous (OAE1a, OAE2) coincide with warm greenhouse climates and extinction events among deep-sea benthic fauna.

The ocean depth below which carbonate minerals dissolve faster than they accumulate — below the CCD (typically ~4,000 m in the modern ocean), no carbonate sediments are preserved. Ocean acidification raises the CCD, causing dissolution of carbonate sediments at shallower depths and recording past acidification events in the geological record.

questions.questionHtml: A sample has a ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio that is 25% of the modern standard ratio (i.e., the sample has lost 75% of its original ¹⁴C). Given that the half-life of ¹⁴C is 5,730 years, approximately how old is the sample?
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. After 1 half-life (5,730 yr): 50% remains. After 2 half-lives (11,460 yr): 25% remains. The sample retains 25% of the original ¹⁴C → 2 half-lives have elapsed → age = 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years.

questions.questionHtml: The Haber-Bosch process now fixes approximately 120 Tg N/year — roughly equal to biological nitrogen fixation. Which of the following is a direct consequence of this massive increase in reactive nitrogen?
options: Increased nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions from agricultural soils, contributing to both radiative forcing and stratospheric ozone depletion
Depletion of atmospheric CO₂ through nitrogen-enhanced plant growth globally, partially offsetting fossil fuel emissions
Acidification of deep ocean waters through nitrogen deposition from the atmosphere
Depletion of atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) leading to reduced partial pressure of N₂ at high altitudes
questions.correctAnswer: Increased nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions from agricultural soils, contributing to both radiative forcing and stratospheric ozone depletion
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. Excess reactive nitrogen (as nitrate and ammonium) in soils is partly denitrified to N₂O by soil bacteria. N₂O is a potent greenhouse gas (GWP₁₀₀ ~265× CO₂) and the dominant current driver of stratospheric ozone depletion (reacting to form NO, which catalyses ozone destruction). Agricultural N₂O is one of the major unresolved climate mitigation challenges.

questions.questionHtml: The silicate weathering thermostat has stabilised Earth’s climate over geological time. A student argues: ‘This means we don’t need to worry about human CO₂ emissions — the thermostat will correct the imbalance.’ Critically evaluate this argument.
options: The thermostat operates on timescales of 100,000–1,000,000 years — far too slow to compensate for human CO₂ emissions on the century timescale, making it irrelevant to the current climate emergency while still being valid geology
The argument is correct — silicate weathering will draw down anthropogenic CO₂ within a few decades and restore pre-industrial conditions
The thermostat only applies to volcanic CO₂ inputs, not to fossil fuel CO₂, so it will have no effect on anthropogenic emissions under any timescale
The thermostat is an untested hypothesis — there is no evidence it actually operates on any timescale
questions.correctAnswer: The thermostat operates on timescales of 100,000–1,000,000 years — far too slow to compensate for human CO₂ emissions on the century timescale, making it irrelevant to the current climate emergency while still being valid geology
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The silicate weathering thermostat is real — it has regulated CO₂ over geological time. But it operates at geological rates determined by weathering kinetics and rock exposure. The current anthropogenic CO₂ forcing is occurring on decadal timescales; the thermostat response is 100,000–1,000,000 times slower. The climate will eventually return to equilibrium — in hundreds of thousands of years. This is not a justification for inaction on human timescales; on human timescales, the thermostat is essentially inoperative.
